strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and topical gap: existing Muon convergence analyses either achieve O(ε^-4) with standard memory, or O(ε^-3) with a large batch size (Muon++), or reduced memory with O(ε^-4) (SUMO); LiMuon is the first in this line to target both a lower memory footprint and O(ε^-3) sample complexity with batch size 1 simultaneously, which is a meaningful algorithmic combination.

The convergence analysis is carried out under both standard Frobenius-Lipschitz smoothness and the more realistic (L0,L1) generalized smoothness condition, which is relevant to LLM training where the gradient-norm-dependent smoothness better matches empirical behavior; this dual treatment (four theorems/settings) is thorough in scope.

The core algorithmic idea—combining STORM-style momentum variance reduction with randomized SVD to compress the momentum state to (m+n)r̂ instead of mn—is simple, practical, and clearly explained with a supporting error-propagation lemma (Lemma 8) tying RSVD approximation error to the true gradient norm.

Experiments span two different architectures/tasks (DistilGPT2 language modeling and ViT image classification) and compare against a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines (Adam, AdamW, Lion, Muon, Muon++, SUMO), with both memory and quality metrics reported.
weaknesses: There is an apparent internal inconsistency between the algorithmic description and the reported experiments: the text explicitly states that 'LiMuon algorithm with Option #1 cannot reduce state memory' (relative to standard Muon), yet Table 2 and Table 3 report LiMuon(#1) using noticeably less memory than Muon and Muon++ (e.g., 6.30GB vs 7.20GB/7.35GB in Table 2). This is not explained and undermines confidence in the memory measurements/methodology.

Assumption 5, needed for the Option #2 (memory-reduced) convergence guarantee, requires that the tail singular-value energy of the momentum matrix is controlled by the true gradient norm — a strong, largely unverifiable structural assumption. The paper criticizes SUMO for relying on 'a strict condition,' but its own low-memory variant rests on a comparably strong and unvalidated assumption, weakening the claimed advantage over SUMO.

The purported benefit of extending the analysis to (L0,L1)-generalized smoothness is undercut by the step-size restriction η ≤ min(1/(2L1 r), β/(8L1 r^{3/2}(1-β))), which forces a small fixed step similar in spirit to the standard Lipschitz case; the analysis does not leverage adaptive/normalized/clipped updates that typically justify studying generalized smoothness, so the practical gain of this extension over Assumption 1 is unclear.

All theoretical rates hide the dependence on r = min(m,n) inside O(·) notation (e.g., rLη/2 terms), yet r can be very large for real weight matrices; the paper does not discuss how this dimension dependence affects the practical iteration/sample complexity, which is important for models with large matrix parameters.

Experimental results are based on single runs without repeated seeds or variance/error bars, despite training curves that are visibly noisy (e.g., Figure 2 test loss spikes). Given that the core selling point is a variance-reduction technique whose benefit is precisely about smoothing stochastic noise, the lack of statistical rigor in the comparison is a notable gap.

No ablation studies are provided for key new hyperparameters introduced by the method (rank r̂, oversampling parameter s, momentum coefficient β) to show sensitivity or memory/performance trade-offs; only one configuration per task is reported.

The experiments are conducted at small scale and low iteration budgets (5000-8000 iterations), and the paper itself acknowledges results are far from state-of-the-art (e.g., PPL ~142-170 vs. the ~18.25 reported elsewhere for DistilGPT2), which limits the strength of the empirical validation of practical usefulness for large-model training, the paper's stated motivation.

The theoretical contribution, while technically executed, is largely a combination of two well-established techniques (STORM variance reduction and randomized SVD) applied to the Muon/nuclear-norm setting rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or analytical insight; novelty is moderate rather than substantial.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and relevant problem: reducing memory footprint of Muon-type optimizers for matrix-structured parameters while improving sample complexity, combining STORM-style variance reduction with randomized SVD.

A reasonably complete convergence analysis is provided for four settings (two algorithmic options x two smoothness assumptions), with detailed proofs in the appendix, extending Muon convergence theory to the generalized (L0,L1)-smooth setting, which prior Muon convergence works largely do not address together with improved O(eps^-3) rates.
The paper is honest about the fact that reported DistilGPT2/ViT results are far from state-of-the-art absolute performance, which is an appropriately transparent limitation statement.
The comparison table (Table 1) clearly summarizes existing Muon variants' complexity/memory trade-offs, giving useful context for positioning the contribution.
weaknesses: The core memory-saving variant (Option #2) critically relies on Assumption 5, which posits that the tail singular value mass of the momentum matrix is bounded by a constant times the true gradient norm. This is a strong, unverifiable, and essentially problem-specific assumption that effectively presumes away the main technical difficulty introduced by low-rank (RSVD) approximation; the convergence guarantee is not meaningful without justifying when/why this holds in practice (e.g., for transformer gradients), and no empirical evidence is given to validate it.

Despite the title emphasizing 'fast,' no wall-clock runtime or throughput comparisons are reported. RSVD introduces non-trivial extra computation per iteration (QR + small SVD), and the paper only vaguely acknowledges 'additional computational cost' without quantifying it, making the 'fast' claim unsubstantiated.

The empirical memory savings are modest and inconsistent with the theoretical claims: Table 2 shows LiMuon(#1), which the text explicitly states 'cannot reduce state memory,' still achieving notably lower memory than Muon (6.30 vs 7.20 GB), while in Table 3 it is nearly identical to Muon (4.09 vs 4.13 GB). This inconsistency is unexplained and undermines confidence in the reported memory numbers.

Experimental evaluation is limited in scale and rigor: training runs are short (5000/~8000 iterations) and far from convergence (perplexities in the hundreds), only single runs are shown with no error bars or multiple seeds, and hyperparameter tuning procedures are described vaguely ('individually tuned for relative optimal performance') without search ranges or protocol details, making it hard to assess robustness of the comparisons.

Several baselines explicitly discussed in Table 1 (SCG, GGNC) are excluded from experiments based on an unverified assumption that they 'behave like standard Muon,' weakening the empirical comparison against the full set of claimed competitors.

The asymptotic rate O(1/T^{1/3}) requires simultaneously setting both learning rate and momentum parameter beta as O(1/T^{2/3}), and in the generalized-smooth case further requires eta to satisfy conditions depending on unknown constants L1, r; these conditions are not actionable for practical hyperparameter selection and are not discussed in relation to the actual experimental hyperparameters used (e.g., constant eta=0.001 and beta=0.05/0.1 in experiments, not vanishing schedules), creating a gap between theory and practice.

The manuscript has noticeable presentation issues, including repeated phrases, grammatical errors, duplicated derivations between the main text and appendix with identical lemma/theorem numbering confusion, and a somewhat convoluted algorithm description (Option #1 and #2 interleaved within a single pseudocode block) that reduces clarity.

The individual technical components (STORM-based variance reduction, randomized SVD, Muon/Newton-Schulz orthogonalization) are all adopted from existing literature; the core novelty lies in their combination, which is incremental rather than a fundamentally new idea, and the significance of the combination is undercut by the issues above.

strengths: The paper provides a fairly complete theoretical treatment, deriving O(ε^-3) SFO complexity for both an Lipschitz-smooth and a generalized (L0,L1)-smooth setting, and for both the full-memory (Option #1) and low-memory (Option #2, RSVD-based) variants of the algorithm, with detailed proofs in the appendix.

The idea of combining STORM-style momentum-based variance reduction with randomized SVD compression of the momentum matrix for Muon-type updates is a sensible and, to my knowledge, new combination that targets both sample complexity and memory simultaneously, whereas prior works (Muon++, SUMO) address only one of these aspects.

Table 1 gives a clear, well-organized comparison against existing Muon variants in terms of SFO complexity, memory, and smoothness assumptions, situating the contribution clearly relative to prior art.

Experiments cover two different architectures/modalities (DistilGPT2 on WikiText-103, ViT on Tiny-ImageNet) and compare against six competitive baselines (Adam, AdamW, Lion, Muon, Muon++, SUMO), with both training curves and tabulated memory/performance numbers.
The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations, e.g., noting that the obtained perplexities do not reach reported state-of-the-art numbers given the limited training budget used.
weaknesses: Assumption 5, which underlies all convergence guarantees for the memory-efficient Option #2 variant (the paper's main selling point), posits that the RSVD truncation error of the momentum matrix is bounded by ρ‖∇f(Wt)‖_F. This is a strong, essentially unverifiable condition tying an algorithmic approximation error to the true gradient norm, and moreover the theorem requires γ ≤ β/(4√r(1-β)) (or a similar condition in Theorem 4), which shrinks as β→0 with T; since γ and ρ are properties of the (fixed) spectral decay of the momentum matrices rather than tunable algorithm parameters, it is unclear whether this condition can be maintained throughout training, raising doubts about whether the stated convergence rate is actually attainable for the memory-efficient variant in practice.

The empirical memory savings are much more modest than the asymptotic claims in Table 1 would suggest (e.g., 7.3GB→6.0-6.3GB for DistilGPT2, and 4.1GB→3.85GB for ViT, i.e., roughly 6-17% reduction), despite the paper emphasizing an (m+n)r̂ ≪ mn asymptotic argument; this gap between theory and practice is not discussed or explained.

LiMuon with Option #1 (the variant that, per the authors' own admission, does NOT reduce memory) achieves by far the best performance in experiments, while Option #2 (the actual memory-efficient variant) underperforms relative to plain Muon on ViT training/testing accuracy; this undercuts the paper's core 'light and fast' claim, since the memory-saving version offers no performance benefit over existing Muon and sometimes performs worse.

No wall-clock time or throughput comparisons are reported, despite 'Fast' being part of the title and the paper acknowledging that RSVD introduces additional computational cost; without this, it is unclear whether the proposed optimizer is actually faster in practice.

Experimental results are based on single runs (no reported variance/seeds), relatively short training horizons (5000-8000 iterations) for small-to-modest sized models (22M-82M parameters), and no ablation on the sensitivity of performance/memory tradeoffs to the key hyperparameters r̂ (target rank) and s (oversampling), despite these being central to the proposed method's claimed benefits.

The core technical ingredients (STORM variance reduction, randomized SVD, Muon's orthogonalized update) are all individually well established; the contribution is primarily in combining and re-deriving the analysis for the matrix/nuclear-norm setting, which, while nontrivial, is somewhat incremental relative to the existing literature summarized in Table 1.

strengths: Novel combination of STORM-style momentum-based variance reduction with randomized SVD for the Muon optimizer, achieving simultaneous improvements in both memory footprint and sample complexity — a nontrivial result since one might expect a memory/accuracy tradeoff.

Comprehensive theoretical treatment: convergence proofs are provided for both exact SVD and Newton-Schulz approximations, under both standard Lipschitz smoothness and generalized (L0,L1)-smoothness, and for both full-memory (Option #1) and low-rank (Option #2) gradient estimators, yielding a consistent O(epsilon^-3) (or O(chi_q^3 epsilon^-3) with Newton-Schulz) rate that improves on the O(epsilon^-4) rates of prior Muon analyses while using (m+n)r-hat memory instead of mn.

Empirical validation spans three distinct architectures/domains (Mamba-130M SSM on WikiText-103, Qwen2.5-0.5B transformer LLM on MiniPile, ViT on Tiny-ImageNet), showing the full-rank LiMuon variant consistently outperforms Muon and Muon++ on perplexity/accuracy, and moderate-rank variants (e.g., rank=16) achieve competitive quality with reduced memory.
Runtime/wall-clock analysis (Table 5) is included, going beyond just sample complexity and memory numbers to give a more complete efficiency picture.
The algorithmic framework and options (Option #1 vs Option #2) are clearly presented with detailed pseudocode, and appendix proofs are extensive and self-contained.
weaknesses: A key comparison baseline, 'Kim & Oh, 2026' (arXiv:2601.19156), is dated in the future relative to the paper's writing and cannot be independently verified at this time; large portions of the Newton-Schulz theoretical contribution (Table 1's second block, Theorems 4.17-4.23) are framed as improvements specifically over this unverifiable reference, which undermines the reader's ability to assess the claimed improvement.

At aggressive low-rank settings (rank=4, sometimes rank=8), LiMuon underperforms plain Muon and even other baselines in absolute quality (e.g., Table 2: LiMuon(rank=4) validation PPL 79.12 vs Muon 71.27; Table 3: LiMuon(rank=4) validation PPL 92.06, worse than Muon's 67.60), indicating that the 'light' memory-saving regime comes with a real, sometimes substantial, quality cost that is understated in the narrative.

The randomized SVD approximation guarantee (Lemma A.4) and the resulting contraction condition (γ ≤ β/(3√r(1-β)) etc. in Theorems 4.11/4.13/4.21/4.23) rely on an assumed bounded tail-singular-value ratio τ that is not empirically verified, and this condition becomes increasingly restrictive as the matrix dimension r grows, creating a tension with the paper's motivation of applying low-rank compression precisely to very large (high-r) matrices.

The per-iteration computational overhead of the RSVD step (Option #2) is acknowledged qualitatively but not incorporated into the complexity or convergence bounds, nor rigorously quantified against the exact-SVD or Newton-Schulz baselines beyond the empirical wall-clock table for one model (ViT).

Training runs are relatively short (2,000-10,000 iterations, small-to-mid-size models up to ~0.5B parameters) which limits confidence that the reported trends (especially memory/perplexity tradeoffs at various ranks) generalize to realistic large-scale pretraining regimes where Muon-style optimizers are actually deployed.

Hyperparameter tuning ranges differ substantially across optimizer families (Table 9), and no code release or artifact is mentioned, which somewhat limits reproducibility verification despite detailed hyperparameter tables being provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: reducing both the sample complexity and memory footprint of Muon-style optimizers for training large models with matrix-structured parameters.

The theoretical analysis is extensive, covering exact-SVD and Newton-Schulz variants, under both standard Frobenius-norm Lipschitz smoothness and the more general (L0,L1)-smoothness, for two different gradient-estimator options (full-rank and low-rank STORM estimates). The proof machinery (STORM-style error recursions, RSVD approximation-error lemmas) is reasonably careful and internally consistent in its algebra.

Combining STORM-type variance reduction with randomized SVD to simultaneously target memory and sample-complexity improvements for Muon is a sensible and largely unexplored combination, and the paper is the first to give convergence guarantees for this combination under both exact SVD and Newton-Schulz approximations.

Experiments span three different architectures (Mamba-130M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, ViT) and several baselines (Adam, AdamW, Lion, SUMO, Muon, Muon++), with full-rank LiMuon consistently outperforming Muon and Muon++ on final perplexity/accuracy metrics, lending some empirical support to the proposed estimator design.
weaknesses: Hidden, unverifiable assumption undermines the central 'low memory + low sample complexity simultaneously' claim: the Option #2 (low-rank) theorems require γ (the RSVD approximation-error ratio) to satisfy γ ≤ β/(3√r(1-β)) (or similar), where γ = τ(1+r̂/(s-1))^{1/2} and τ is the (data-dependent, uncontrollable) tail-singular-value energy ratio of the momentum matrix. Since the optimal schedule sets β = O(1/T^{2/3}) → 0, satisfying this constraint for a *fixed* rank r̂ effectively requires τ → 0 as training proceeds, i.e., it implicitly assumes the momentum matrices become increasingly well-approximated by rank r̂ as T grows. This assumption is never stated explicitly as a hypothesis and is not discussed or justified; without it, the claimed O(ε^-3) rate for the lower-memory variant is not actually guaranteed at a fixed, practical rank r̂. This is a material gap between the theoretical story and the practical algorithm as implemented (where r̂ is fixed at 4/8/16 regardless of T).

Despite the title 'Light and Fast,' the low-rank variants are not faster in wall-clock terms: Table 5 shows LiMuon(r̂=4/8/16) has higher per-step time than Muon and takes longer wall-clock time to reach a target loss than full-rank Muon (e.g., 10-12 min vs 7 min), because RSVD introduces nontrivial overhead. The 'fast' claim in the title/abstract is thus only supported by the full-rank variant, not by the memory-efficient variants that are the paper's main selling point.

The practical memory savings are modest relative to the asymptotic (m+n)r̂ vs mn claim: e.g., for Mamba-130M, rank-4 LiMuon only saves ~17% total GPU memory versus full precision baselines (18.86 GB vs 22.80-22.92 GB), likely because reported numbers include activation/model memory, not just optimizer state, so the headline complexity comparison in Table 1 (optimizer state memory only) overstates the real-world benefit.

The core technical contribution is an incremental combination of two well-established techniques (STORM-style momentum variance reduction, already used in Muon++, and randomized SVD, already used in SUMO) rather than a fundamentally new estimator or analysis technique; the paper's claimed 'first' results are mostly a matter of combining existing tools in a new but fairly straightforward way.

Performance of the memory-efficient (low-rank) variants is inconsistent and sometimes clearly worse than existing Muon/Muon++ baselines (e.g., on Qwen2.5-0.5B, LiMuon rank=4 has validation perplexity 92.06, substantially worse than Muon's 67.60 and even worse than SUMO's 88.73), which weakens the practical case for the method at the memory-saving operating points that are supposedly its main selling point.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small models (130M, ~500M, and 22M parameters) trained for limited iterations (2,000-10,000 steps), which is modest for a paper framed around 'training large models'; it is unclear whether the claimed benefits (both memory and convergence speed) persist at the billion-parameter scale where Muon-type optimizers are typically most impactful.

The paper's presentation is extremely repetitive: eight nearly identical convergence theorems/proofs are given for all combinations of {Lipschitz, generalized smoothness} x {exact SVD, Newton-Schulz} x {Option 1, Option 2}, with proofs following essentially the same template; this could have been consolidated into one or two general theorems with corollaries, improving readability and making it easier to spot the shared underlying assumptions (including the γ/τ issue above).

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the Muon optimizer literature: combining momentum-based variance reduction (STORM-style) with randomized SVD to jointly target sample complexity and memory footprint, which prior variants (Muon++, SUMO) address only separately.

Comprehensive theoretical treatment: convergence proofs are provided for 8 distinct settings (exact SVD vs. Newton-Schulz approximation, two memory options, and two smoothness assumptions—standard Lipschitz and generalized (L0,L1)-smoothness), with explicit rates of O(ε^-3) and O(χ_q^3 ε^-3), improving on the O(ε^-4) rates of most prior Muon analyses.
Empirical evaluation spans three different architectures/modalities (Mamba-130M SSM, Qwen2.5-0.5B Transformer LLM, ViT for vision), which is more diverse than most Muon-variant papers.

Ablations over rank (4/8/16/full) illustrate the memory-performance tradeoff concretely, and a wall-clock runtime/time-to-target analysis (Table 5) is included, which is often missing in similar optimizer papers.

The proofs in the appendix are detailed and self-contained, with careful handling of the coupling between the variance-reduction recursion and the low-rank approximation error via Lemma A.4 (RSVD error bound).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of two existing techniques (STORM variance reduction and randomized SVD/Halko et al. compression) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the 'first study' claims, while arguably accurate, somewhat overstate the degree of originality.

The practical memory savings are modest when LiMuon matches or exceeds Muon/Muon++ performance: e.g., in Table 2, LiMuon(rank=16) needs 22.31GB (vs. Muon++'s 22.35GB) to reach comparable/better perplexity, and in Table 3 the memory gap between full-rank LiMuon and Adam/Muon is under 10%; the low-rank variants that achieve meaningful memory reduction (rank=4) show substantial performance degradation relative to full-rank or even plain Muon, undermining the headline 'simultaneously lower memory and lower complexity' claim in practice.

Runtime results (Table 5) show LiMuon is slower per-step than vanilla Muon (24.75–26.87ms vs 23.43ms) due to RSVD overhead, and only the full-rank variant achieves the best time-to-target, which is at odds with the 'fast' framing in the title; low-rank variants do not show a convincing speed advantage.

No experiments at genuinely large model scale (billions of parameters) despite the paper's framing around 'large models'; the tested models (130M–500M) are modest, leaving open whether the memory/complexity benefits persist or amplify at scale where they would matter most.

The SUMO baseline's limitation (bounded objective assumption) is used to dismiss it as a fair low-memory comparator, but SUMO still achieves competitive or better memory savings in some experiments (e.g., Table 2/3), and the paper does not quantitatively show LiMuon dominates it on a joint memory-performance Pareto front.

Hyperparameter settings (e.g., oversampling parameter s, learning rates) differ across models and methods without clear justification or sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility concerns; the search ranges in Table 9 suggest substantial tuning effort that may not transfer easily to new settings.

The remarks following each theorem are highly repetitive (near copy-paste across the 8 theorem sections), which bloats the paper without adding insight; the presentation could be condensed substantially without loss of content.

The convergence rate improvement from O(ε^-4) to O(ε^-3) relies on standard STORM-style variance reduction machinery already used in Muon++ (Sfyraki & Wang, 2025); the paper's genuine new content is primarily the integration of RSVD and its error propagation analysis, which is a comparatively narrow technical delta.
